pool.q: A 60-year-old female presents with recurrent scleritis. She has no significant past medical history other than some chronic joint inflammation of the hands and feet and ulnar deviation of her fingers. What laboratory test would most likely reveal the underlying cause of her scleritis?
pool.rationale:
This patient likely has rheumatoid arthritis. Serologic testing is important in the workup and diagnosis of RA. Rheumatoid factor (RF) is present in 70%–80% of patients. Anti-nuclear antibodies are elevated in many inflammatory diseases. Antiphospholipid antibodies are seen in lupus and other rheumatic diseases. Anti-SS-A antibody tests, along with tests for anti-SS-B antibodies, are used in the detection of Sjögren syndrome.


Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is the most common rheumatic disorder, affecting approximately 1% of adults worldwide, and is 3 times more likely to occur in ­women than in men. RA is classically a progressive, symmetric, and deforming peripheral polyarthritis characterized by synovial inflammation and hypertrophy as well as autoantibody production. Although it can involve any joint, RA primarily affects the small joints of the hands and feet. Typically, affected joints are swollen and tender, with decreased range of motion and deformity from bone and cartilage destruction. Hand deformities (Fig 9-1) include nodules, ulnar deviation, Boutonnière deformity (abnormally flexed proximal interphalangeal [PIP] joint and extended distal interphalangeal [DIP] joint), and swan-­neck deformity (abnormally hyperextended PIP and flexed DIP). Early diagnosis and treatment are critical in controlling the joint damage and associated disability.

Extra-­articular Manifestations
Extra-­articular involvement, which is an indicator of disease severity, occurs in about 40% of RA patients over the course of the illness. Risk ­factors for systemic involvement include the presence of rheumatoid ­factor (RF), anti–­cyclic citrullinated peptide (CCP) antibodies, and smoking. RA can affect almost all systems; manifestations include
  • subcutaneous rheumatoid nodules (in approximately 25% of patients)
  • anemia of chronic disease (common in RA patients)
  • increased risk of lymphoma
  • Felty syndrome (seropositive RA, neutropenia, and splenomegaly)
  • osteopenia and a higher risk of fractures
  • pleural effusions, pulmonary nodules, and interstitial fibrosis
  • cardiac disease (coronary artery disease, pericarditis and effusions, valvular disease from rheumatoid nodules, and cardiomyopathy from secondary amyloid deposition)
  • peripheral vascular disease and vasculitis (small-­ to medium-­sized vessels)
  • carpal tunnel syndrome (from synovitis, compressive myelopathy, or radiculopathy)
  • muscle weakness (primary or drug-­induced myopathy)
Ocular involvement may include dry eye disease, scleritis, episcleritis, and corneal inflammation, melting, and infection. The ocular manifestations of RA are discussed in BCSC Section 8, External Disease and Cornea, and Section 9, Uveitis and Ocular Inflammation.

Laboratory Testing
Serologic testing is impor­tant in the workup and diagnosis of RA. Rheumatoid ­factor (RF) is pres­ent in 70%–80% of patients. However, it has limited specificity for the disease, as it can be positive in up to 10% of unaffected individuals and in about one-­third of patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Anti-­CCP antibody is as sensitive as RF but has a higher specificity for RA (98%). Nevertheless, both of ­these tests may be negative in up to 50% of RA patients. Similarly, anti–­mutated citrullinated vimentin (anti-­MCV) antibody testing shows high specificity for the disease. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-­reactive protein (CRP) levels are usually elevated. Antinuclear antibody (ANA) testing is nonspecific, ­because only 30% of RA patients have positive results, but it can help exclude other diseases such as SLE. Although ge­ne­tic testing is not performed routinely, the HLA-­DRB1 gene appears to be the strongest known ge­ne­tic risk ­factor for the development of RA.

Treatment
Treatment of RA involves an integrated approach, incorporating medi­cations and nondrug therapies. Nonpharmacologic interventions include dietary counseling, exercise, physical therapy, smoking cessation, lipid control (to reduce the associated cardiovascular risks), and immunizations (to reduce the risk of infection linked with the use of immunosuppressive agents).
The ultimate goal of pharmacologic treatment (discussed in detail at the end of this chapter) is disease remission. Early diagnosis and treatment are imperative in preventing or delaying the long-­term effects of disease progression. Mild symptoms of joint stiffness and pain can be treated with analgesics and nonsteroidal anti-­inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), although ­these agents do not alter the long-­term prognosis. Glucocorticoids are sometimes helpful in controlling the acute stages of inflammation; severe cases may require sustained low-­dose therapy (<10 mg/day).
Disease-­modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs), which are divided into nonbiologic and biologic agents, have been shown to slow disease progression, reduce potential joint destruction, and maintain joint function while also limiting the need for long-­term ste­roid use. In addition to their anti-­inflammatory effect, ­these drugs reduce the body’s heightened autoimmune reaction. Thus, the clinician should consider screening for pre­existing infectious conditions such as hepatitis B and C and tuberculosis. Among nonbiologic agents, methotrexate is generally the first-­line treatment, but other options are available. Biologic agents, developed through ge­ne­tic engineering, are modified proteins that can target cytokines. The largest group of currently available agents consists of anti–­tumor necrosis ­factor (TNF)-­a inhibitors. Other biologics act by blocking interleukin (IL)-1 or IL-6 receptors or in modifying T-­cell or B-­cell activity. One emerging group of DMARDs, which are technically small-­molecule drugs as opposed to true biologic agents, targets the inhibition of the Janus kinase (JAK) enzyme involved in mediating inflammation.

pool.q: What medication is associated with blue-yellow color defects?
pool.rationale:
Digoxin is associated with disturbances of color vision, usually blue-yellow pattern defects. The resulting experience can be described as a yellow, green, blue, or red tinge to objects. Some patients also experience glare phenomena, yellow or green flickering vision, or formed visual hallucinations.
Some patients who use amiodarone report hazy vision and colored halos around lights. Corneal whorl-like deposition is common. Amiodarone optic neuropathy can also cause slow progressive bilateral vision loss.
Lisinopril can cause orbital angioedema. Metoprolol can cause keratoconjunctivitis sicca-like syndrome, likely due to decreased lacrimation.

Ophthalmic considerations
Many of the adult patients seen and treated by ophthalmologists are in the age group at risk for IHD and its many complications. They often undergo stressful eye surgery ­under local or general anesthesia, and ophthalmologists need to be cognizant of ­these patients’ risks of myo­car­dial ischemia, myo­car­dial infarction, CHF, and arrhythmias. Similarly, ophthalmologists need to be aware of the association between proliferative diabetic retinopathy and IHD. This information should be given to the primary medical care provider of patients with proliferative diabetic retinopathy but no diagnosis of IHD so that appropriate screening tests can be considered.
Cardiac complications of noncardiac surgery are a major cause of perioperative morbidity and mortality, MI being the most significant. Older
age, preexisting CHD, and CHF are the principal risk ­factors for development
of ­these complications.
ICDs are increasingly used for the management of cardiac arrhythmias. Although no cases of discharge of an ICD during ocular surgery have been reported, the ophthalmologist should discuss the status and pos­si­ble perioperative disabling of the ICD with the cardiologist or anesthesiologist before ocular surgery to avoid surgical complications.
Fi­nally, ophthalmologists should be aware of the potential ocular adverse effects associated with medi­cations commonly used in treating CVD. Following are the medi­cations of clinical relevance:
  • Amiodarone. Corneal microdeposits occur in nearly all patients who use amiodarone for an extended period of time (years). The corneal epithelial whorl-­like deposition is indistinguishable from that due to chloroquine. Visual changes are unusual; patients most often report hazy vision or colored halos around lights. Photosensitivity reactions from amiodarone may lead to discoloration (usually slate gray or blue) of periocular skin. A rare adverse effect is amiodarone optic neuropathy, which is characterized by an insidious onset, slow progression, bilateral vision loss, and protracted optic nerve head swelling that tends to stabilize within several months of discontinuing the medi­cation. Patients on long-­term amiodarone therapy should have a baseline ophthalmic examination, follow-up examinations ­every 6–12 months, and immediate evaluation of any new visual disturbances. ­Because of this drug’s photosensitizing effects, UV-­blocking spectacle lenses should be considered in selected cases of chronic eyelid disease or macular disease.
  • b-­Blockers. The use of some b-­blockers can lead to a keratoconjunctivitis sicca–­like syndrome, prob­ably due to decreased lacrimation. They may also possibly enhance migraine ocular scotomata and may decrease intraocular pressure (IOP). Topical b-­blockers, particularly timolol, may be less effective in lowering IOP in patients concurrently taking systemic b-­blockers. Visual disturbances and vivid visual hallucinations may also be associated with the systemic use of b-­blockers.
  • Digoxin. Glare and disturbances of color vision are the most common and striking ocular adverse effects. They include decreased vision and prob­lems with color vision, such as blue-­yellow pattern defects; a yellow, green, blue, or red tinge to objects; and colored halos (mainly blue) around lights. Patients on digoxin may also describe yellow or green flickering vision, colored borders around objects, glare phenomena, light flashes, scintillating scotomata, a frosted appearance to objects, and formed visual hallucinations.
  • ACE inhibitors. ­These agents may cause angioedema involving the eye and orbit. The presumed mechanism is the disruption of bradykinin metabolism.

pool.q: What percentage of human blood composition is made of formed elements (red blood cells, leukocytes, platelets)?
pool.rationale: Formed ele­ments—­erythrocytes (red blood cells, or RBCs), leukocytes (white blood cells), and platelets—­constitute approximately 45% of the total blood volume. The fluid portion, plasma, is about 90% ­water. The remaining 10% of the plasma consists of proteins (albumin, globulin, fibrinogen, and enzymes), lipids, carbohydrates, hormones, ­vitamins, and salts. If a blood specimen is allowed to clot, the fibrinogen is consumed, and the resultant fluid portion is called serum.

Warfarin is a vitamin K antagonist that reduces the synthesis of numerous clotting factors that require vitamin K. Aspirin blocks cyclo-oxygenase and inhibits platelet aggregation. pool.q: A 65-year-old woman with symmetric bilateral arthritis presents with ulnar deviation and a positive anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody test. What ocular manifestation is commonly associated with this systemic disease?
pool.rationale: The question describes a patient with rheumatoid arthritis (RA). Scleritis, episcleritis, and corneal melting are commonly associated with rheumatoid arthritis. Although other areas of the eye can be inflamed in the eyes of patients with RA, these are not typical associations. Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (CCP) antibody has recently been used in the classification of RA and has been shown to be more specific than rheumatoid factor (RF) for the diagnosis of RA. Retinal vasculitis is often seen in antineutrophil cytoplasmic autoantibody (ANCA)-associated diseases, including Behçet disease, but is not common in patients with RA. Optic neuritis is most commonly regarded as clinically isolated or associated with demyelinating disease such as multiple sclerosis. Trabeculitis may be seen in patients with glaucomatocyclitic crisis or HSV-associated anterior uveitis, but is not typical in patients with RA.

pool.q: What is the most radiosensitive structure in the eye?
pool.rationale: In general, radiation and chemotherapy have their greatest effects on mitotically active tissue. As a result, the most radiosensitive structure in the eye is the lens. This is followed, in order, by the cornea, the retina, and the optic nerve. As the retina is not an actively growing tissue, radiation retinopathy can take years to develop and develops from damage to vascular endothelium. Radiation damage may be enhanced by concomitant chemotherapy or concomitant systemic disease states, such as diabetes mellitus or hypertension.

pool.q: What class of antihypertensive medications should be avoided in patients with reactive airway disease?
pool.rationale:
ß-blockers can cause bronchospasm and should thus be avoided in patients with asthma and reactive airway disease. They also cause bradycardia and should be avoided in patients with second- and third-degree atrioventricular blocks. In patients with heart failure due to systolic dysfunction, the use of certain ß-blockers reduces hospitalization for heart failure and improves survival rates. ß-blockers are beneficial in the treatment of atrial fibrillation and essential tremor.
While ACE inhibitors may cause a dry cough in 5%-20% of patients, reactive airway disease is not a contraindication. ACE inhibitors should be avoided in patients with a history of angioedema or known renal artery stenosis (RAS). They are contraindicated in pregnancy, and in patients trying to become pregnant, because of the adverse effects on fetal renal function and risk of fetal death.
Nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers should be avoided in patients with cardiac conduction abnormalities such as atrial fibrillation or heart failure associated with left ventricular dysfunction and in patients with acute MI.

pool.q: A 72-year-old man with a past medical history of a myocardial infarction and placement of a cardiac stent 7 months ago presents for preoperative evaluation for cataract surgery. He is taking aspirin and clopidogrel. The surgical plan is for a clear corneal incision approach with topical anesthesia. What is the most appropriate recommendation to the patient for the management of his dual antiplatelet therapy?

options.a: He may continue taking aspirin but should discontinue clopidogrel several days prior to surgery.
options.b: He may continue taking aspirin and clopidogrel.
options.c: His surgery should be delayed until 1 year has elapsed since his cardiac event.
options.d: He should discontinue both aspirin and clopidogrel several days prior to surgery.

pool.rationale:
The decision to maintain or discontinue anticoagulants or antiplatelet agents for ophthalmic surgery is contingent on the type of procedure, the bleeding risk, the effect of bleeding on postoperative outcome, and the risk of a serious or fatal thrombotic event after discontinuation. For uncomplicated cataract surgery via clear corneal incision under topical anesthesia, the benefit of discontinuing anticoagulants to prevent bleeding does not outweigh the potential risks.
Studies found an increased risk of ophthalmic bleeding when warfarin was continued in patients undergoing cataract surgery, but the bleeding events were minor and did not impact vision. Continuation of aspirin or clopidogrel had similar findings. Direct-acting anticoagulants (eg, factor Xa inhibitors [apixaban, edoxaban, rivaroxaban] and a thrombin inhibitor [dabigatran]) have a 20% lower risk than warfarin of causing intraocular bleeding during surgery. In an emergent situation, the monoclonal antibody idarucizumab can reverse the effect of dabigatran within 15 minutes. In patients on dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin plus clopidogrel) after cardiac stent placement, there is increased risk of thrombosis of the stented artery, with potentially fatal outcome if these agents are discontinued.
Cataract surgery may be performed in these patients when cessation of anticoagulants is felt to be unnecessary. For other ocular surgeries in which a successful outcome may be impacted by intraocular or periocular bleeding, some surgeons prefer to stop therapy; in those cases, elective surgery may need to be delayed for up to 1 year to avoid adverse thrombotic events.

pool.q: A 28-year-old woman has intermediate uveitis, which reactivates with associated macular edema, reducing visual acuity below 20/40 every time her prednisone dosage is reduced below 15 mg per day. She recently learned that she is pregnant. From the perspective of systemic health, what option represents the safest way to manage the intermediate uveitis?

options.a: maintaining a 15 mg dosage of oral prednisone every day throughout the pregnancy
options.b: periocular injections of triamcinolone acetonide every 2.5 months
options.c: adding cyclophosphamide as a corticosteroid-sparing agent
options.d: adding methotrexate as a corticosteroid-sparing agent

pool.rationale:
There is an almost complete absence of randomized clinical trials to guide decision making in the case of a pregnant or lactating patient. However, the best evidence from case series, animal studies, and expert opinion favors a general approach of utilizing the lowest dosage of the least toxic medication available. In a patient with uveitis, use of a local corticosteroid in the form of drops or injections would result in the least amount of medication exposure to the fetus.
Systemic corticosteroid use would result in greater exposure, although this approach can be successful and is often utilized with careful supervision by the obstetrician.
Antimetabolites, such as methotrexate, are known teratogens and are absolutely contraindicated during pregnancy or in those who may soon become pregnant. Similarly, alkylating agents, such as cyclophosphamide, are absolutely contraindicated during pregnancy, and the potential negative effects on fertility should be taken into consideration in all patients of child-bearing age.

pool.q: A college freshman is brought to the emergency department with fever, headache, neck stiffness, and altered mental status. The patient's lower extremities demonstrate diffuse petechiae. What antibiotic prophylaxis is most appropriate to prescribe for contacts of the patient for the most likely causative organism of this clinical presentation?
pool.rationale:
This vignette is alluding to bacterial meningitis caused by the organism Neisseria meningitidis (meningococcus). Meningococcus is a gram-negative diplococcus. In young adults, serogroup B is the most common pathogen, which can cause epidemics, especially among close-quartered populations. The high virulence of this organism is partially enabled by the polysaccharide capsule and endotoxin within its cell wall. While the treatment for the infection is classically high-dose penicillin, rifampin or minocycline are typically used for chemoprophylaxis for those that have been in contact with the patient. One of the unique ocular side effects of rifampin is pink-tinged tears, in addition to blepharoconjunctivitis.
Clindamycin is primarily used to treat anaerobic infections and is useful for its coverage of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). Cefalexin is a first-generation cephalosporin that is often used to treat skin, bone and joint, and genitourinary infections. Ciprofloxacin is a second-generation fluoroquinolone antibiotic that is often used to treat gastrointestinal and genitourinary infections.

pool.q: Nearly all isolates of Haemophilus influenzae are now resistant to what antibiotic class?
pool.rationale:
In general, the treatment of Haemophilus influenzae has been complicated by the emergence of resistant strains. Nearly all strains of H influenzae are resistant to macrolides, and more recent reports note decreased sensitivity to cephalosporins and quinolones. In some geographic regions, ampicillin resistance to H influenzae is nearing 50%.
The most current recommendation for empiric treatment of H influenzae are third- generation cephalosporins, which are highly effective against H influenzae infections. Alternative treatments include meropenem or ampicillin and chloramphenicol. Sensitivity testing should guide further treatment.
Recall, H influenzae is a common inhabitant of the upper respiratory tract in 20% to 50% of adults and 80% of children. Encapsulated species, with increased protection against phagocytosis, are more capable of systemic spread. There are 6 serotypes, with a conjugate vaccination available to type b (Hib). In fully immunized populations, Hib has been nearly eradicated with a significant decline in the rates of meningitis, orbital cellulitis, and other Hib-related infections (arthritis, otitis media, bronchitis, etc).

pool.q: What is the sensitivity of enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) testing to support the clinical diagnosis in the early stages of Lyme disease?

options.a: ELISA testing will be only 20% sensitive during the early stages of Lyme disease.
options.b: ELISA testing is 75% sensitive during the early stages of Lyme disease.
options.c: ELISA testing is 95% sensitive during the early stages of Lyme disease.
options.d: ELISA testing will be only 50% sensitive during the early stages of Lyme disease.

pool.rationale:
Lyme disease, which is caused by the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi, occurs in 3 stages: Skin manifestations such as erythema chronicum migrans represent the initial, localized disease (stage 1). Disseminated disease (stage 2) manifests as flulike illness. Persistent disease (stage 3) consists of nervous and cardiac involvement. Serologic testing such as enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) should be used to support the clinical diagnosis and not as a primary basis for treatment. ELISA testing is 50% sensitive in the early stages; however, almost all patients test positive in later stages.
Treatment of B burgdorferi infection depends on the stage and severity of the infection. Early Lyme disease is typically treated with oral doxycycline, amoxicillin, cefuroxime, or erythromycin. Mild disseminated disease is treated with oral doxycycline or amoxicillin. Serious disease (with cardiac or neurologic manifestations) is typically treated with ceftriaxone or high-dose penicillin G for up to 6 weeks.

pool.q: What virus is the most common reason for liver transplants in the United States?
pool.rationale:
At present, hepatitis C virus (HCV) is the most common cause of liver cancer and the most common indication for liver transplantation in the United States. Because of direct hepatocyte cytotoxicity, HCV causes the most damage of all the hepatitis viruses in immunocompetent hosts. It may cause cirrhosis, fulminant hepatitis, and hepatocellular carcinoma.
Hepatitis A is the leading cause of hepatitis in the US; it usually does not cause long-term liver damage. Hepatitis B can cause cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma, which kill 20% and 5% of patients, respectively. Hepatitis D causes chronic delta hepatitis, which is a severe form of chronic liver disease.

pool.q: What are hallmarks of schizophrenia?

options.a: disorientation or memory loss caused by any disease, drug, or trauma directly affecting the central nervous system
options.b: elevated mood sufficiently severe to cause impairment in functioning
options.d: persistent low mood and slowed thought processes

pool.rationale: The hallmarks of schizophrenia include hallucinations, delusions, disorganized thinking, and negative symptoms such as emotional and cognitive blunting and social and occupational dysfunction. Motor disturbances range from uncontrolled, aimless activity to catatonic stupor, in which the patient is immobile, mute, and unresponsive yet fully conscious. Repetitive, purposeless mannerisms and an inability to complete goal-directed tasks are also common. Patients might have other mental health conditions such as depression or anxiety disorders, but these are not essential features of the disease.

pool.q: A 73-year-old man presents with a mild preseptal cellulitis of the left lower eyelid, for which he is prescribed oral clindamycin. Two days later, the patient is seen in follow-up, with significant improvement in eyelid erythema and edema. Five days later, the patient calls the ophthalmologist's office complaining of fever and non-bloody diarrhea. What diagnostic test would be most appropriate?
pool.rationale:
This vignette presents a case of Clostridium difficile colitis ("C-diff"). The causative organism is an anaerobic, gram-positive bacillus, which is spore-forming and part of the normal gastrointestinal flora. C-diff commonly occurs in the setting of antibiotic use, as in this case of preseptal cellulitis treated with clindamycin. This antibiotic diarrhea features fever and abdominal discomfort, and the diarrhea may be watery or occasionally bloody. Clindamycin is a common offending antibiotic, along with cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones, and tetracyclines. The bacterium elaborates cytopathic toxins (A and B), which can be detected by ELISA, and is typically treated with metronidazole or oral vancomycin. A polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assay is also sometimes used in the diagnosis of Clostridium difficile colitis.
Stool osmolality, ova and parasites, and culture are all used in the work-up of diarrhea, but in the setting of fever and recent antibiotic usage, C difficile colitis is the most likely diagnosis.

pool.q: Elevated blood pressure, elevated levels of fasting plasma glucose, elevated triglyceride levels, low high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol levels, and what other finding characterize the diagnostic criteria for metabolic syndrome?

pool.q: A 20-year-old patient with a history of seizures presents for a general eye examination. During the examination, the patient loses consciousness, and on subsequent electroencephalogram (EEG) testing with her neurologist is found to have abnormal activity in both hemispheres. What type of seizure did the patient experience in the ophthalmologist's office?
pool.rationale: Generalized seizures cause impaired consciousness and abnormal activity in both hemispheres of the brain at the onset of the seizure. They can be nonconvulsive (absence, or "petit mal") or convulsive (tonic-clonic, or "grand mal"). They may follow a partial seizure. Partial seizures are limited to only 1 part of the brain and further subdivided into simple (without impairment of consciousness) and complex (with impairment of consciousness) seizures. Simple partial seizures are associated with symptomatic auras. Adults with epilepsy most commonly experience complex partial seizures. During these seizures, the patients may appear awake but do not follow instructions or interact.

pool.q: A 65-year-old man with diabetes and hypertension is brought to the emergency department 2 hours after the onset of weakness on the right side. What imaging study is the most important in guiding acute management?
pool.rationale:
Multiple studies have shown that the administration of the fibrinolytic agent recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (rtPA) within a 3-hour window of symptom onset results in lower morbidity from ischemic strokes. Imaging with noncontrast head computed tomography (CT) is critical in evaluating for the presence of hemorrhage, which would be a contraindication to rtPA use.
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is more sensitive than CT in detecting evolving ischemia within hours of onset, particularly if diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) MRI with apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) mapping is used. However, MRI is too time-intensive, considering the limited window during which rtPA can be administered. Cerebral angiography provides detailed information about vascular abnormalities, but it is not indicated in the acute setting and would not reveal either stroke or hemorrhage. Transcranial Doppler ultrasonography may reveal stenosis of the intracranial arteries but is not helpful in making decisions regarding initial management.

pool.q: A patient with refractory seizures has been prescribed vigabatrin. What screening test should be performed before treatment is initiated?

A visual field test must be performed before initiating therapy to exclude the possibility of preexisting visual field loss, then repeated every 3 months. None of the other studies (VEP, electro-oculography, OCT) have been shown to be of value for screening, nor are they validated for the detection of vigabatrin-associated visual field loss.

pool.q: A former nurse presents with a white cornea, blurred vision, a central corneal abrasion, and minimal to no pain. pool.q: What is the most common type of thrombosis that occurs in patients with antiphospholipid antibody syndrome (APS)?

pool.q: An infant is born with microcephaly. Ocular examination reveals bilateral retinal pigment epithelium mottling and areas of chorioretinal atrophy.  The mother reports travel to Brazil several months ago. Congenital infection with what virus is most likely?

The constellation of microcephaly, pigment mottling, and travel to Brazil is suggestive of congenital Zika virus infection. Zika virus is a single-stranded RNA virus of the Flaviviridae family. The natural vector is the female Aedes aegypti mosquito. Many adults infected with Zika virus are asymptomatic, but they may experience nonspecific symptoms such as fever, conjunctivitis, rash, and joint pain. The classic triad of congenital rubella syndrome features sensorineural deafness, variable ocular abnormalities (including cataracts, salt-and-pepper retinopathy), and congenital heart abnormalities. Cytomegalovirus and herpes simplex virus type 2 are less associated with congenital syndromes.

pool.q: What drug always should be available when performing edrophonium chloride testing (to evaluate for myasthenia gravis), in case excess cholinergic stimulation occurs?

Therefore, whenever the test is to be performed, a syringe containing 0.5 mg of atropine sulfate should be available. If signs of excess cholinergic stimulation occur, then the atropine should be administered intravenously, and the dose may be repeated every 3 to 10 minutes, as needed.
The other drugs listed are not recommended to treat excess cholinergic stimulation. Epinephrine may be added to local anesthetic to prolong the duration of anesthesia, as well as to decrease intraoperative bleeding. Hyaluronidase may be added to local anesthetics for retrobulbar injection, to reduce the risk of myotoxicity from the anesthetic agents. Pyridostigmine (Mestinon) is an oral treatment for myasthenia gravis.

pool.q: What medication used to treat Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection causes pink-tinged tears and blepharoconjunctivitis?

pool.q: What is the most commonly elevated auto-antibody found in patients with Graves hyperthyroidism (thyroid eye disease)?

pool.q: What immunosuppressant medication should be considered as a last option in a 15-year-old female with diabetes mellitus and bilateral, vision-threatening, HLA-B27-associated panuveitis?

Cyclophosphamide is a potent immunosuppressive drug that, given its potential to cause sterility, is reserved for recalcitrant disease, especially in young patients of childbearing age. There are ocular side effects with long-term use of corticosteroids orally, including cataract development and intraocular pressure elevation.
Corticosteroids are often used in the acute setting for patients with severe uveitis. Patients who are diabetic require close monitoring of blood glucose levels to prevent hyperglycemic episodes. Methotrexate and infliximab are frequently used, often in combination, to treat uveitis in the pediatric population. Methotrexate is a dihydrofolic acid reductase inhibitor. It can be hepatotoxic after prolonged use. It is renally excreted and should be used with caution in patients with impaired renal function. Infliximab is a TNF-alpha blocker and can cause immunosuppression as well as cytopenia.

pool.q: What is the life span of a circulating red blood cell?

Hormones such as erythropoietin, thrombopoietin, and granulocyte colony-stimulating factor initiate the differentiation of the various cellular elements. The life span of a circulating RBC is 120 days.

pool.q: What blood pressure (BP) measurement indicates stage 2 hypertension?
pool.rationale:
Blood pressure staging should be based on an average of 2 or more seated BP readings during 2 or more visits.
  • normal BP is defined as a systolic <120 mm Hg and diastolic <80 mm Hg
  • elevated BP is defined as a systolic 120-129 mm Hg and diastolic <80 mm Hg
  • stage 1 hypertension is defined as a systolic 130-139 mm Hg OR a diastolic 80-89 mm Hg
  • stage 2 hypertension is defined as a systolic ≥140 mm Hg OR a diastolic ≥90 mm Hg

pool.q: What HbA1C value would be diagnostic of prediabetes?
pool.rationale:
Prediabetes is characterized by one of the following:
  • HbA1C of 5.7%-6.4%
  • fasting plasma glucose (FPG)  level of 100-125 mg/dL
  • oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) plasma glucose level of 140-199 mg/dL 2 hours after intake of a 75-gram glucose load.
Diabetes mellitus is diagnosed by one of the following:
  • HbA1C level of ≥ 6.5%, reflecting average levels of blood glucose over 3 months
  • fasting plasma glucose (FPG) level of ≥126 mg/dL
  • oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) plasma glucose level of ≥ 200 mg/dL 2 hours after intake of a 75-gram glucose load.
  • symptoms of diabetes mellitus (polyuria, polydipsia, fatigue, weight loss) and a random plasma glucose level of ≥200 mg/dL.
Normal HbA1C is < 5.7%. HbA1C levels diagnostic of diabetes mellitus are ≥ 6.5%. It is important for the managing ophthalmologist to be aware of HgA1C levels, as a 1 percentage reduction in HbA1C can reduce the risk of retinopathy by 30%.

pool.q: What group of patients with juvenile idiopathic arthritis is most likely to have ocular involvement?

Furthermore, a positive antinuclear antibody (ANA) test result in either of these 2 groups is associated with an increased risk of developing uveitis. Psoriatic and enthesitis-related arthritis were added to help in categorizing patients who did not fit into more common entities. Uveitis can occur in both of these subtypes.

pool.q: A patient presents with slowly worsening, painless, bluish-gray flat pigmentation of the temporal sclera in the left eye. There is no scleral thinning. What medication should the ophthalmologist look for on their medication list?
pool.rationale:
Minocycline is a tetracycline-class antibiotic that can cause painless blue-gray or brown hyperpigmentation of the skin, nails, oral cavity, skeleton, thyroid, cardiac valves, and eye. Accumulation of pigment is generally dose-dependent and may improve with drug cessation.
Alendronate sodium is a bisphosphonate, a type of disease-modifying agent that has been reported to cause scleritis, orbital inflammation and myositis, anterior uveitis, and/or conjunctivitis. Patients with prior episodes of necrotizing anterior scleritis or scleromalacia perforans (a painless form of necrotizing anterior scleritis) may have a blue-gray-brown appearance to the sclera due to scleral thinning and exposure/visibility of the underlying uveal tissue. This patient did not have thinning.
Ciprofloxacin and topiramate do not cause scleral pigmentation. Ciprofloxacin has the following ocular adverse effects: exacerbation of myasthenia, visual sensations, and retinal detachment.
Topiramate has the following ocular adverse effects: abnormal accommodation, photophobia, strabismus, anterior uveitis, acute myopia, anterior chamber shallowing, secondary angle-closure glaucoma, visual field defects, and suprachoroidal effusions.

pool.q: What is a recommended treatment for Haemophilus influenzae infection?

pool.q: A patient with bilateral granulomatous uveitis is suspected to have sarcoid. Under what circumstance can a diagnosis be made without requiring histopathology?

pool.q: A 54-year-old woman presents with intermittent eyelid edema over the past several months that is bilateral, symmetric, nontender, and worse in the morning. For 2 months, she has had occasional heart palpitations. She has not begun any new medications. What is the recommended management of this patient'?

pool.rationale:
The etiology of orbital inflammation can be infectious, autoimmune, vasculitic, granulomatous, or nonspecific. This patient's inflammation does not appear to have an infectious or toxic origin, which narrows down the differential of eyelid edema. Thyroid eye disease (autoimmune) should always be high in the differential for noninfectious orbital inflammatory disease, and fluctuating eyelid edema is a typical ocular sign for TED. While bilateral intermittent eyelid edema may be of allergic etiology, the history provided does not lead the examiner toward an allergic cause, and a patient with concurrent heart palpitations is more likely to have a diagnosis of thyroid disease. Therefore, thyroid function testing would be a better choice in the initial management of this patient's condition.
It is important to remember that while this patient’s eyelid edema is described as symmetric, thyroid eye disease is frequently asymmetric. Furthermore, the severity of clinical findings does not parallel the patient’s serum thyroid studies. Finally, bilateral upper eyelid dermatochalasis necessitating blepharoplasty would not be an intermittent symptom, and thus blepharoplasty does not fit for the management of this patient. If a thyroid patient does require surgery, the usual order is orbital decompression, followed by strabismus surgery, followed by eyelid surgery.

pool.q: What component of the adaptive immune system is responsible for complement-mediated bacterial killing?
pool.rationale: The immune system of multicellular organisms is divided into 2 components: (1) innate immunity, which has a broad specificity and provides a nearly immediate response to pathogens, and (2) adaptive immunity, which involves immune memory of prior exposure and, therefore, usually is slower to respond, due to the time required for specific immune cell clones to proliferate. From there, the immune system can be further categorized into (1) humoral and (2) cellular components. The humoral system is made of cells derived from B lymphocytes and is responsible for antibody-mediated opsonization, complement-mediated bacterial killing, antitoxin, and mediation of intracellular infections. The cellular immune system is derived from T lymphocytes and has different functions. Mechanical defenses provide a direct physical barrier against pathogens.

pool.q: The complication of respiratory distress following Nadbath block, an injection into the stylomastoid foramen that is used to provide facial akinesia, occurs by what mechanism?

pool.rationale:
Respiratory distress and dysphagia can occur when the anesthetic agent is injected too deeply into the area of the facial nerve as it exits the stylomastoid foramen. Anesthetic bathes cranial nerves IX, X, and XI as they exit the jugular foramen, resulting in paralysis. The patient may become dysphagic, hoarse, start coughing, or develop stridor or severe respiratory insufficiency. Treatment includes supportive measures until the anesthetic is metabolized.
Thin patients are more at risk for this complication, because the needle is more likely to be placed too deeply into their skin. To avoid such issues, a short hypodermic needle can be used and a small volume injected (<3 mL).
Allergic bronchospasm and direct injury to the larynx are unlikely with proper technique and review of the patient's medical history, including drug allergies. Inadvertent subdural injection can occur during retrobulbar block and accidental needle contact with the optic nerve sheath.

pool.q: A patient with Neisseria gonorrhoeae urethritis must also be treated for coinfection with what organism?

pool.q: What is the function of oncogenes?

pool.q: Carotid endarterectomy (CEA) is recommended for patients with recent (within 6 months) transient cerebral ischemia (TCI) or ischemic stroke and what percentage of ipsilateral carotid artery stenosis?

  • For patients with recent (within the past 6 months) TCI or ischemic stroke and severe (70%–99%) ipsilateral carotid artery stenosis, CEA is recommended if the perioperative morbidity and mortality risk is less than 6% and the patient’s life expectancy is greater than 5 years.
  • For patients with recent cerebrovascular events and moderate ipsilateral stenosis (50%–69%), CEA is recommended, depending on patient- specific factors such as age, sex, and other comorbidities.
  • There is no benefit of CEA or CAS in a patient with stenosis of less than 50%.
  • Surgery may be performed within 2 weeks of a TCI or stroke.
  • CAS can be considered as an alternative to CEA in symptomatic patients when the patient is at low risk for endovascular intervention and an internal carotid artery stenosis of greater than 70% is indicated by noninvasive imaging or an internal carotid artery stenosis of greater than 50% is indicated by catheter angiography. CAS may also be considered in other selected patients.
In addition to cerebral conditions, ocular conditions such as transient monocular vision loss (TMVL) and retinal TCIs can be associated with carotid stenosis. The ophthalmologist is often the first physician to see a patient with TMVL; the TMVL is usually embolic, with either a carotid or a cardiac source. The annual stroke rate among patients with isolated TMVL, retinal infarcts, or TCIs is approximately 2%, 3%, and 8%, respectively. Untreated individuals with TMVL, retinal infarcts, or TCIs have a 30% risk of MI and an 18% risk of death over a 5- year period.

The following approach should be considered for a patient presenting with a cerebral or retinal transient ischemic attack (TIA):
  • emergency department or urgent outpatient evaluation or hospital admission if the event occurred within the previous 48 hours
  • patient evaluation for the presence of risk factors associated with atherogenesis:hypertension, diabetes mellitus, obesity, hyperlipidemia, and smoking
  • institution of appropriate medical therapy
  • evaluation by appropriate testing for the presence of a cardiac source of emboli
  • determination using duplex ultrasonography of the possibility of carotid stenosis

pool.q: What study is preferred to confirm that retinopathy is associated with carotid occlusive disease?
pool.rationale:
Carotid duplex ultrasonography is relatively inexpensive, quick, and noninvasive, with high sensitivity and high specificity for diagnosing high-grade carotid stenosis. However, ultrasonography may overestimate the degree of stenosis and is less accurate in individuals with less than 69% stenosis. The accuracy of the results is also very much operator-dependent, resulting in high variability among different ultrasound laboratories. If the ultrasonography findings suggest the need for surgical intervention, it may be prudent to confirm with a second imaging modality.
Magnetic resonance angiography is more expensive than carotid ultrasonography and cannot be done in patients who are unable to assume a supine position or in those who have ferromagnetic implants and/or pacemakers. However, the 3-dimensional image of the carotid artery produced by MRA is useful in diagnosing high-grade carotid stenosis and provides an anatomic complement to carotid ultrasonography.
Computed tomography angiography (CTA) is superior to carotid ultrasonography for differentiating high-grade carotid stenosis from total occlusion and effectively excludes carotid stenosis that is greater than 70%, making CTA useful as a screening test. If there is disagreement between MRA and carotid ultrasonography results, CTA is useful in adjudicating the findings. Cerebral angiography remains the gold standard imaging modality for patients with suspected carotid occlusive disease, but its invasive nature and associated morbidity and mortality risk limits its applicability.

pool.q: What should pregnant women avoid to reduce risk of infection by Toxoplasma gondii?

Also, pet owners should keep cats indoors, where they are less likely to eat infected prey and subsequently acquire T gondii.

pool.q: A healthy 52-year-old former nuclear submarine engineer asks whether his prior occupation exposed him to any health risks. What ocular complication associated with radiation exposure is most likely to be observed on slit-lamp examination?
pool.rationale:
The lens is the most radiosensitive structure in the eye, followed by the cornea, the retina, and the optic nerve. Cataract formation is the most likely complication of radiation exposure that would be found in this patient; specifically, posterior subcapsular cataracts. Low doses of radiation (as low as 2 Gy in 1 fraction) may cause cataract formation, and higher doses of radiation (7–8 Gy and higher) can cause progressive cataracts. The average latent period for the development of radiation-induced cataracts is 2 to 3 years.
In severe cases, erosion of the corneal epithelium and secondary ulceration may result. Radiation retinopathy clinically resembles diabetic retinopathy; injury occurs first to the capillary vascular endothelium, then the capillary pericytes, and then the endothelium of larger vessels, resulting in ischemic changes. Cotton-wool spots develop first, followed by capillary nonperfusion, then ingrowth of telangiectatic vessels. Radiation optic neuropathy may present with optic nerve head pallor and splinter hemorrhages, but the exposure may also be clinically silent except for symptoms of unilateral headache and ocular pain.

pool.q: What drug is the most effective for treatment of pseudomonal infections?

Cephalexin is a first-generation cephalosporin and cefuroxime is a second-generation cephalosporin; both have some activity against gram negative organisms, but are not effective for Pseudomonas.

pool.q: What is the most frequent cause of death of patients suffering shock?

pool.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with visually significant cataracts. A preoperative evaluation indicates her blood pressure is 185/95. pool.q: What varicella-zoster vaccine may be safe for use in immunocompromised patients?

pool.q: What is the most common psychiatric problem in older adults?
pool.rationale:
Depression is the most common psychiatric problem in the geriatric population, affecting one-fourth of older adults seen in the primary care setting. Patients who are visually impaired have even higher rates of depression. For example, 30%-40% of patients with macular degeneration have depression.
Suicide is not isolated to younger age groups. Indeed, American men older than 65 are 5 times more likely to commit suicide than the general population. The most common cited reason is loneliness. Older American women are more likely to attempt suicide but are less often successful.
Signs of depression in the elderly population include change in appetite, agitation, decreased libido, weight changes, loss of energy, difficulty concentrating, feelings of worthlessness or guilt, and recurrent thoughts of death or suicide.
Compared to younger populations, older depressed patients are more likely to express hypochondriacal complaints, minimize symptoms of depression, and have psychotic delusional disease. They are less likely to express guilt.
The ophthalmologist must know how to recognize these symptoms and signs and refer patients for further evaluation. Red flags may include unexplained vision loss and frequency of visits to the ophthalmology office.

pool.q: Bisphosphonates used to treat osteoporosis have been associated with what eye condition?

Angle-closure glaucoma can be caused by anti-cholinergic agents such as atropine or scopolamine and adrenergic agents such as epinephrine. Sulfa drugs can also cause angle-closure glaucoma through ciliary body edema, causing anterior rotation of the lens-iris diaphragm.
Age-related macular degeneration is not associated with any medication.

pool.q: What clinical finding is most characteristic of secondary syphilis?
pool.rationale:
A syphilis infection starts as primary syphilis with a small ulcerated painless papule called a chancre, which heals spontaneously in 6 weeks. Within a few weeks after the chancre heals, patients can develop secondary syphilis, which is heralded by a truncal rash that may spread over the entire body. Uveitis occurs in approximately 10% of secondary syphilis cases.
If untreated, patients can develop latent syphilis, which has no symptoms. Of those patients with latent syphilis who do not receive treatment, 15%-30% will develop tertiary (late) syphilis, wherein the disease damages various organ systems, including the central nervous system (CNS), and is characterized by destructive granulomatous lesions with a typical endarteritis. Uveitis occurs in approximately 5% of tertiary syphilis cases.
Ocular syphilis can occur at any stage of syphilis. Ocular syphilis manifests most commonly as posterior uveitis or panuveitis, but it can also present with interstitial keratitis, anterior uveitis, optic neuropathy, and retinal vasculitis.
Treatment for syphilis depends on the stage and CNS involvement. Ocular syphilis and neurosyphilis are treated with either aqueous crystalline penicillin G IV or procaine penicillin IM with probenecid for 10-14 days.

pool.q: A 40-year-old male presents with a mild bilateral conjunctivitis with a mucopurulent discharge. On further questioning, he started having dysuria a few weeks ago that was followed by pain in his left knee and ankle. Given this information, laboratory testing was performed that revealed a positive HLA-B27 result. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
The classic triad of reactive arthritis includes arthritis, urethritis, and conjunctivitis. HLA- B27 and genetics appear to be involved in susceptibility to developingreactive arthritis after an infection. Males are affected 2–3 times more often than females. The arthritic symptoms typically have their onset from days to weeks after the antecedent infection. Up to 40% of patients with either AS or reactive arthritis develop the typical manifestations of acute nongranulomatous iridocyclitis, which can be recurrent and bilateral. Ocular involvement tends not to correlate with the activity of the joint disease. Culture- negative bilateral conjunctivitis, which is typically self- limited, is also a common manifestation of reactive arthritis.
Ulcerative colitis and ankylosing spondylitis are also associated with a positive HLA-B27 test result, but the presentations of these diseases are different than that of reactive arthritis, and they are not associated with urethritis. Rheumatoid arthritis is not associated with urethritis.

pool.q: A patient presents with bilateral conjunctival telangiectasia and has a history of bloody tears that resolve. A review of systems elicits a history of painless gastrointestinal bleeding. What condition should be suspected?
pool.rationale:
The answer is hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia. All of the listed diseases have both ocular and gastrointestinal manifestations. Only hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Rendu-Osler-Weber disease) is associated with spontaneous subconjunctival hemorrhage and intermittent, painless gastrointestinal bleeding. Furthermore, patients can have vascular abnormalities of the skin, nasal and oral mucosa, lung, and brain. The conjunctival telangiectasias are sharply circumscribed, elevated, and composed of arborizing dilated channels. The subconjunctival hemorrhages can occasionally cause bloody tears.
Ulcerative colitis is also associated with gastrointestinal bleeding but is not associated with spontaneous subconjunctival hemorrhages. The ocular manifestation of this inflammatory bowel condition is usually anterior uveitis. Other, less common, ocular changes include conjunctivitis, episcleritis, central serous choroidopathy, and choroiditis.
Gardner syndrome is a combination of Familial Adenomatous Polyposis and Congenital Hypertrophy of the Retinal Pigment Epithelium (CHRPE). The presence of 4 or more CHRPE lesions increases the likelihood of familial polyposis. These patients should have gastrointestinal (GI) screening as the adenomas may undergo malignant transformation. Gardner syndrome does not have an association with subconjunctival hemorrhages.
Abetalipoproteinemia (Bassen-Kornzweig, AR) is a retinitis pigmentosa syndrome that is due to an inability to transport and absorb lipids leading to a deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, and K). The clinical findings of abetalipoproteinemia include ataxic neuropathy, growth retardation, coagulopathy, Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) fundus findings, and Bitot’s spot. The workup includes abetalipoprotein B blood test, complete blood cell (CBC) count, cholesterol studies, and stool sample. Treatment involves large doses of fat-soluble vitamin supplementation.

pool.q: What stage of Treponema pallidum infection is characterized by fever, lymphadenopathy, patchy hair loss, and malaise?
pool.rationale:
The initial inoculation of Treponema pallidum (syphilis) occurs through intact mucous membranes or abraded skin and, within 6 weeks, results in a broad, ulcerated, painless papule called a chancre. The spirochetes readily enter the lymphatic system and bloodstream. The ulcer heals spontaneously, and signs of dissemination appear after a variable quiescent period of several weeks to months.
The secondary stage is heralded by fever, malaise, adenopathy, and patchy loss of hair. Maculopapular lesions may develop into wartlike condylomata in moist areas, and oral mucosal patches sometimes appear. All of these lesions are highly infectious. The secondary lesions may resolve in a few weeks or may relapse in the first year. Without treatment, the disease enters the latent stage.
Latent syphilis, characterized by positive serologic results without clinical signs, is divided into 2 stages. The early latent stage occurs within 1 year of infection. During this time, the disease is potentially transmissible, because relapses associated with spirochetemia are possible. The late latent stage is associated with immunity to relapse and resistance to infectious lesions.
Tertiary manifestations can occur from 2 to 20 years after infection, and one-third of untreated cases of latent disease progress to this stage. The remaining two-thirds of cases either are subclinical or resolve spontaneously. Tertiary disease is characterized by destructive granulomatous lesions with a typical endarteritis that can affect the skin, bones, joints, oral and nasal cavities, parenchymal organs, cardiovascular system, eyes, meninges, and central nervous system (CNS).

pool.q: A new patient is referred for evaluation of mydriasis in both eyes, which was noticed only by the patient's spouse. The pupils are equal, round, and reactive to light. pool.q: What levels of low-density lipoproteins (LDL) and high-density lipoproteins (HDL) are recommended to decrease the risk of cardiovascular disease?

pool.q: A 34-year-old patient has strabismus surgery under general anesthesia. During the procedure, he develops tachycardia, a rise in body temperature, and muscular rigidity. What is the preferred treatment of this condition?

options.c: cool skin with ice and administer benzodiazepine
options.d: release tension on extraocular muscles and administer atropine

Typically, the first sign of MH is unexplained elevation of end-tidal carbon dioxide concentration. The treatment includes immediately discontinuing surgery and anesthetic agents, hyperventilating with oxygen, and administering dantrolene.
Benzodiazepines, cooling, and beta blockers are not part of the initial therapy. Releasing extraocular muscles and administering atropine is the treatment of the oculocardiac reflex, not malignant hyperthermia.

pool.q: What antiepileptic medication is associated with bilateral acute angle closure?

pool.q: A 15-year-old girl who has had a renal transplant complains of a right-sided headache for 2 days. Herpes zoster virus infection occurs when varicella-zoster virus in the dorsal root and cranial nerve ganglia reactivates. Pain in a sensory nerve distribution may be the first sign of reactivation. Topical antivirals are only effective in the treatment of epithelial mucoid plaques or more chronic epithelial disease. Topical steroids are indicated for keratouveitis. Oral steroids, a controversial treatment aimed at reducing postherpetic neuralgia, is contraindicated in immunocompromised patients.

pool.q: A young patient with hypertension is being evaluated for secondary causes. What etiology would delayed or absent femoral pulses suggest?

Coarctation of the aorta is characterized by a narrowing of the aorta and can cause delayed or absent femoral pulses.
Hyperaldosteronism will cause a decrease in potassium levels in the absence of treatment with a diuretic (or a large drop with low-dose diuretic treatment). Pheochromocytoma should present with a flank mass, and renovascular disease would produce a unilateral abdominal bruit in a younger patient with severe end-organ disease on presentation.

It typically manifests with sudden-onset headache, nausea, vomiting, and varying degrees of impaired consciousness. pool.q: What skin finding is most characteristic of primary syphilis?
pool.rationale:
A syphilis infection starts as primary syphilis, with a small ulcerated painless papule called a chancre, which heals spontaneously in 6 weeks. Within a few weeks after the chancre heals, patients can develop secondary syphilis, which is heralded by a truncal rash that may spread over the entire body. Uveitis occurs in approximately 10% of secondary syphilis cases.
If untreated, patients can develop latent syphilis, which has no symptoms. Of those patients with latent syphilis who do not receive treatment, 15%-30% will develop tertiary (late) syphilis, wherein the disease damages various organ systems, including the central nervous system (CNS), and is characterized by destructive granulomatous lesions with a typical endarteritis. Uveitis occurs in approximately 5% of tertiary syphilis cases.
Ocular syphilis can occur at any stage of syphilis. Ocular syphilis manifests most commonly as posterior uveitis or panuveitis, but it can also present with interstitial keratitis, anterior uveitis, optic neuropathy, and retinal vasculitis.
Treatment for syphilis depends on the stage and CNS involvement. Ocular syphilis and neurosyphilis are treated with either aqueous crystalline penicillin G IV or procaine penicillin IM with probenecid for 10-14 days.
